newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Dips in gold lease rates may signal more gold.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Dips in gold lease rates may signal more gold.

text.p: Recent downward gold lease rate movements could be indicating new supplies of the precious metal are entering the market, gold dealers said on Thursday.

Implied one-month lease rates, currently around 1.18 percent, dipped to their lowest levels in several months on Wednesday in intraday trading to around 1.07 percent, suggesting to analysts there was little speculative selling of bullion taking place.
Dealers said another reason for falling lease rates may be that more gold is being offered for lending.
"What it may be saying is that there's suddenly more gold out there," one dealer for an international bank said.

However, while the potential exists for more gold entering the marketplace via central banks, which globally hold some 35,000 tonnes in reserves, the dealers said they were unaware of any such occurrences lately.
There was also little to suggest mining houses were feeling inclined to unwind forward sales positions, given widespread negative sentiment on the direction of the gold price.
In Australia, where most mining houses run active hedge books, the trends is rather to increase forward sales to lock in future earnings.
At the end of 1996, Australian producers had 22.5 million ounces hedged forward, up from 20 million in the previous year figures from accountants Coopers and Lybrand show.
Gold, which typically performs best in times of economic and political uncertainties, has fallen out of a favour with some investors as Wall Street continues to deliver profits.
The potential for future sales by Switzerland's central bank, the Swiss National Bank, was discounted by dealers as a potential cause of dipping lease rates, given the time frame for any disposals.

Switzerland would not be able to start selling gold before 1999 to finance a planned human rights foundation and other national projects, the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and Swiss commercial bankers said on Wednesday.

The Swiss government proposed last week creating a seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian foundation that would sell revalued official gold reserves over 10 years to raise money for victims of poverty, human rights abuses and the Holocaust.
